name: Primer
tagline: Where numbers come alive for curious kids
description: Primer is a visual math learning platform for children ages 6-12 that transforms abstract concepts into interactive, colorful adventures. Kids don't just memorize formulas — they discover mathematical thinking through play, puzzles, and stories that make every concept stick.
mission:
Most children don't hate math. They hate feeling lost. The moment a kid falls behind — misses a concept, gets confused by notation, or simply zones out during a lecture — math becomes a wall instead of a window. And traditional approaches respond with more worksheets, more drilling, more of exactly what made them disengage in the first place.

Primer was built by a team of former math teachers, game designers, and child psychologists who believe that mathematical thinking is as natural to children as language. Watch any five-year-old sort their Halloween candy or argue about who got the bigger slice of pizza — they're already doing math. The problem isn't ability, it's presentation.

Our platform turns every math concept into something you can see, touch, and play with. Fractions become pizza slices you actually divide. Multiplication becomes building blocks you stack into arrays. Geometry becomes treasure maps you navigate. Every interaction is designed around the way children's brains actually process spatial and numerical information — through pattern recognition, visual reasoning, and narrative context.

We work alongside school curricula rather than replacing them. Teachers assign Primer as practice and exploration, and our dashboard shows them exactly which concepts each student has internalized and which need more time. Parents see their kids asking to do math before bed — not because we've gamified it with hollow rewards, but because we've made it genuinely fascinating.

Our north star is a generation of kids who see math not as a subject to survive, but as a superpower to wield. Every child deserves to feel the thrill of a pattern clicking into place.
marketResearch:
The K-12 edtech market reached $28 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at 16% CAGR through 2030. Within this, math-specific learning platforms represent approximately $5.2 billion, driven by persistent achievement gaps — only 36% of U.S. fourth graders tested proficient in math on the 2024 NAEP assessment. Our SAM of $1.8 billion focuses on supplemental math tools for elementary students in English-speaking markets. Our initial SOM targets U.S. households with children 6-12 and progressive elementary schools, representing roughly $240 million.

The competitive landscape includes established players like Khan Academy Kids (free, broad but not math-focused), Prodigy Math (game-based but relies on extrinsic rewards over genuine understanding), and DreamBox (adaptive but visually dated and enterprise-focused). Newer entrants like Photomath focus on homework help rather than conceptual understanding. Primer differentiates through its visual-first pedagogy — every concept is taught through spatial manipulation and interactive models rather than video lectures or drill-and-kill exercises.

Our primary customer segments are parents of elementary-age children seeking engaging math support (average willingness to pay $12-20/month for educational apps) and elementary schools looking to supplement core curricula with adaptive practice tools. The parental anxiety around math achievement creates strong demand — 78% of parents report concern about their child's math preparation.

Our GTM motion combines organic virality (kids sharing progress with classmates) with targeted digital advertising to parents of 6-8 year olds during back-to-school and report card seasons. School adoption follows a teacher-champion model: free classroom accounts convert to district licenses when principals see engagement data.

name: Fluent
tagline: Talk your way to fluency with AI conversation partners
description: Fluent pairs language learners with AI conversation partners that adapt to their level, interests, and goals. Instead of memorizing vocabulary lists, learners practice real dialogue — ordering coffee in Paris, negotiating in Mandarin, or debating philosophy in German.
mission:
The language learning industry has a dirty secret: most people who complete a course still can't hold a conversation. They can conjugate verbs on paper but freeze when a taxi driver asks where they're going. The gap between classroom knowledge and real-world fluency is enormous, and traditional apps have made it worse by optimizing for streak counts instead of speaking confidence.

Fluent exists because the only way to learn to speak is to speak. Our AI conversation partners simulate the messy, unpredictable, context-rich experience of talking to a real person — complete with slang, cultural nuances, and the occasional misunderstanding. They're patient when you struggle, challenging when you're ready, and always available at 3am when insomnia and ambition collide.

What makes our approach different from a chatbot is depth. Each AI partner has a persona, a backstory, and opinions. You're not practicing with a translation engine — you're having coffee with Sophia, a Roman architect who is passionate about urban design and will absolutely correct your subjunctive. The emotional engagement of genuine conversation is what makes language stick.

We build on decades of second-language acquisition research showing that comprehensible input — language slightly above the learner's current level — drives fluency faster than any other method. Our AI calibrates every response to sit in that sweet spot, pushing learners just enough to grow without overwhelming them into silence.

Our vision is a world where anyone can become conversationally fluent in a new language within six months, without ever booking a flight or finding a conversation partner. The technology is finally here. We're making it accessible.
marketResearch:
The global language learning market hit $67 billion in 2025, growing at 18% CAGR. Digital language learning specifically represents $22 billion, with mobile-first platforms dominating consumer spend. The AI-powered conversation practice segment is nascent but growing rapidly as LLM capabilities improve. Our TAM is $22 billion in digital language learning, SAM is $6.5 billion targeting adults learning the top 10 global languages via mobile apps, and our initial SOM is $350 million focused on English speakers learning Spanish, French, German, Japanese, and Mandarin.

Duolingo dominates with 100M+ monthly active users but is widely criticized for producing learners who can match pictures to words but struggle in real conversations. Babbel and Rosetta Stone offer more structured curricula but lack adaptive conversation practice. Italki and Preply connect learners with human tutors at $15-40/hour — effective but expensive and scheduling-dependent. Fluent occupies the gap: conversation-first practice at app pricing, available 24/7.

Our target users are motivated adults (25-45) learning a language for career advancement, travel, or personal enrichment. This demographic spends an average of $180/year on language learning and values speaking ability over test scores. Secondary segments include expatriates needing rapid functional fluency and professionals preparing for international roles.

GTM strategy starts with a freemium app offering 3 free conversations daily, converting to $16/month for unlimited practice and advanced personas. Viral growth comes from shareable conversation highlights and a referral program offering bonus conversation credits. B2B expansion targets corporate language training programs, replacing expensive tutor-based programs with scalable AI practice.

name: Meridian
tagline: The management training your company forgot to give you
description: Meridian is a leadership development platform designed specifically for first-time managers. Through cohort-based programs, 1-on-1 AI coaching, and real-world practice exercises, new managers learn to lead teams with confidence instead of faking it until they break.
mission:
Every year, millions of talented individual contributors get promoted into management with virtually no preparation. One day you're writing code or closing deals, and the next you're responsible for other people's careers, performance reviews, and emotional well-being. The assumption is that being great at your job means you'll be great at managing others. This assumption is catastrophically wrong.

Meridian was founded by three first-time managers who learned leadership the hard way — through painful feedback, lost team members, and years of trial and error that could have been compressed into months with the right guidance. We're building the training program we wish had existed on the day we first heard the words "you're the new team lead."

Our curriculum is ruthlessly practical. We don't teach leadership theory or make people read case studies about Jack Welch. We teach the specific, tactical skills that first-time managers need in their first 90 days: how to run a productive one-on-one, how to give feedback that doesn't destroy trust, how to manage someone who was your peer yesterday, how to have the performance conversation you've been dreading.

Every lesson comes with a practice exercise that managers complete with their actual team. Learn about effective delegation on Tuesday, practice it with a real project on Wednesday, debrief with your cohort on Thursday. The learning loop is tight, contextual, and immediately applicable.

We believe that good management is the single highest-leverage investment a company can make. One great manager affects eight to twelve people every single day. We're here to create more of them, faster.
marketResearch:
The corporate leadership development market is valued at $58 billion globally, yet most spending goes to senior executive programs. The specific segment of first-time manager training is underserved, representing roughly $8 billion in annual spend despite being the most critical transition point in any professional's career. Research from Gartner shows that 60% of new managers underperform in their first two years. Our SAM of $3.2 billion targets mid-market and enterprise companies in North America and Europe. Our SOM of $280 million focuses on tech companies with 200-5,000 employees where IC-to-manager transitions are frequent.

Competitors include BetterUp (coaching platform, $300-500/person/month, focused on senior leaders), Hone (live group training, broad leadership topics), and LinkedIn Learning (self-paced video, no practice or cohort component). Internal L&D teams often build ad hoc programs that vary wildly in quality. Meridian differentiates through its exclusive focus on first-time managers, its practice-with-your-real-team methodology, and its cohort model that creates peer accountability.

Our primary buyer is the VP of People or Head of L&D at companies experiencing rapid growth, where the number of new managers is outpacing the organization's ability to train them. The average company promotes 15-20 new managers per year. At our per-seat pricing, this represents $15K-45K in annual contract value — well within departmental budgets.

Our GTM starts with a self-serve tier for individual managers who are investing in themselves, building brand awareness and collecting testimonials. Enterprise sales follow, targeting HR leaders through content marketing, conference sponsorships, and a network of HR advisors who recommend Meridian during organizational scaling.

name: Chalk
tagline: Flashcards that write themselves, schedules that actually work
description: Chalk is a spaced repetition platform that uses AI to generate high-quality flashcards from any source material — lecture notes, textbooks, PDFs, or even YouTube videos. Combined with a scientifically-optimized review schedule, Chalk ensures you remember everything you study.
mission:
Every student knows they should use flashcards and spaced repetition. The research is overwhelming — it's the most effective memorization technique ever studied. And yet most students don't use it, or they start and quit within a week. The reason is simple: creating good flashcards is tedious, and maintaining a review schedule requires discipline that vanishes during midterm season.

Chalk removes both barriers. Drop in your lecture slides, paste a textbook chapter, or link a YouTube lecture, and Chalk generates a complete flashcard deck in seconds — not just simple term-definition pairs, but cards that test understanding through cloze deletions, scenario questions, and conceptual connections. The AI doesn't just extract facts; it understands what's worth remembering and how to test for genuine comprehension.

Once your cards exist, Chalk's scheduling algorithm takes over. Built on a modernized version of the SM-2 algorithm enhanced with machine learning, it predicts exactly when you're about to forget each card and schedules a review at the optimal moment. Study ten minutes a day and retain months of material. The system learns your personal forgetting curves and adapts — everyone's memory works differently, and your schedule should too.

We're particularly focused on medical students, law students, and language learners — communities where the volume of memorization is immense and the stakes of forgetting are real. But the principles apply to anyone who needs knowledge to stick: certification preppers, professionals learning new domains, or curious people who are tired of reading books and remembering nothing.
marketResearch:
The digital flashcard and study tool market is valued at $3.8 billion, anchored by Quizlet's 60M monthly active users. The broader test prep and study aid market reaches $12 billion. Spaced repetition specifically is experiencing a renaissance driven by evidence-based learning advocates on social media and the growing demands of professional certification programs. Our TAM encompasses the $12 billion study tool market, SAM of $4.2 billion targets digital-first students and professionals in English-speaking markets, and SOM of $180 million focuses on medical students, law students, and IT certification preppers.

Quizlet dominates flashcards but lacks intelligent scheduling — reviews are random, not spaced. Anki is the gold standard for spaced repetition but has an interface from 2006 and requires manual card creation that takes longer than studying itself. RemNote and Mochi bridge the gap partially but lack AI card generation. Chalk is the first platform to combine Anki-grade scheduling algorithms with AI-powered card generation and a modern mobile-first interface.

Our primary users are medical students (1.1M in the U.S. alone, spending an average of $200/year on study tools), followed by law students, engineering students, and IT professionals pursuing certifications. These users face enormous memorization loads and are highly motivated to adopt evidence-based study methods. The medical student community in particular has a strong culture of tool-sharing, creating natural viral distribution.

GTM strategy leverages the study tool influencer ecosystem on YouTube and Reddit. We sponsor popular study-with-me creators and provide free premium accounts to student ambassadors. Organic growth comes from shared decks — when one med student creates a pharmacology deck, their entire class adopts Chalk to study it.

name: Orbit
tagline: A science experiment on your doorstep, every month
description: Orbit delivers monthly hands-on science experiment kits to kids ages 5-14, paired with a digital companion app that extends each experiment into deeper learning. From building volcanoes to growing crystals to coding simple robots, every box turns kitchens into laboratories.
mission:
Science education has a paradox. Kids are natural scientists — they ask why the sky is blue, how magnets work, and what would happen if you mixed everything under the kitchen sink. But by middle school, most of them think science is boring. Somewhere between their natural curiosity and the standardized curriculum, the magic gets squeezed out.

Orbit was created to protect that magic. Every month, we deliver a box that turns a kid's kitchen table into a laboratory. Inside is everything they need for a real experiment — not a craft project disguised as science, but a genuine investigation with a hypothesis, variables, and results that might actually surprise them. The baking soda volcano has its place, but we go further: kids extract DNA from strawberries, build simple circuits, grow bacterial cultures, and engineer bridges that hold real weight.

What makes Orbit different from other subscription boxes is the depth. Each kit comes with a companion app that extends the experiment into the underlying science. After building an electromagnet, kids explore how MRI machines use the same principles. After growing crystals, they learn how geologists study mineral formation. We connect the hands-on experience to the bigger scientific picture, building genuine understanding rather than just a fun afternoon.

We calibrate every kit for safety, mess tolerance, and adult involvement. A five-year-old can do most experiments with a parent nearby. A twelve-year-old can run them independently. The goal is autonomy — we want kids to feel like scientists, not like they're following instructions. Each kit includes open-ended extension challenges that push curious kids to design their own experiments.

Our dream is that every Orbit kid arrives at their first high school chemistry class already knowing what a hypothesis is, already comfortable with failure, and already hooked on the thrill of discovering something new.
marketResearch:
The children's educational subscription box market is valued at $4.2 billion, growing at 22% CAGR as parents increasingly seek alternatives to screen time. STEM-focused boxes represent approximately $1.4 billion of this market. Our TAM encompasses the $4.2 billion educational box market, our SAM of $1.8 billion targets STEM boxes for English-speaking families with children 5-14, and our SOM of $150 million focuses on households in the U.S. and UK with above-median income and children in the target age range.

KiwiCo is the dominant player with an estimated $200M+ in annual revenue across multiple age-segmented lines (Kiwi Crate, Tinker Crate, etc.). MEL Science focuses on chemistry with strong production quality but narrow scope. Little Passports covers geography rather than STEM. Orbit differentiates through the digital companion app that transforms a physical kit from a one-afternoon activity into weeks of extended learning, and through our focus on real scientific methodology rather than craft-oriented projects.

Our target customer is the "science-curious parent" — typically college-educated, household income above $80K, with children ages 5-10 as the primary entry point. These parents value educational enrichment and are willing to spend $25-40/month on quality STEM activities. Retention in subscription boxes averages 6-8 months; Orbit targets 10+ months by making each kit a building block that connects to previous experiments.

GTM strategy combines Instagram and YouTube influencer partnerships with targeted Facebook ads during gifting seasons (birthdays, holidays, back-to-school). Gift subscriptions represent 35% of initial purchases and convert to self-subscriptions at a 28% rate. School partnerships — where teachers recommend Orbit as supplemental home science — provide a trusted endorsement channel.

name: Folio
tagline: Assessment that showcases what students can actually do
description: Folio is a portfolio-based assessment platform for creative programs — design, art, writing, film, and architecture schools. Instead of reducing student work to letter grades, Folio lets students curate digital portfolios that demonstrate growth, process, and mastery to instructors and future employers.
mission:
Creative education has an assessment problem. You can't reduce a design thesis to a B+. You can't capture the evolution of a filmmaker's visual language in a percentage score. Yet most creative programs still rely on traditional grading systems that were designed for multiple-choice exams, forcing instructors to flatten nuanced, subjective evaluation into a number that tells students almost nothing about their growth.

Folio reimagines assessment for disciplines where the work is the evidence. Our platform lets students build living portfolios throughout their program — uploading projects, documenting process, reflecting on decisions, and receiving structured feedback from instructors and peers. Assessment happens through rubric-based evaluation directly on the portfolio, creating a rich record of growth that a transcript could never capture.

For instructors, Folio solves the logistics nightmare of creative assessment. Instead of juggling USB drives, email attachments, and physical submissions, everything lives in one platform with inline annotation tools, customizable rubrics, and cohort-wide analytics that reveal patterns in student development. Faculty spend less time on administration and more time on the mentorship that actually matters.

For students, the portfolio they build in Folio becomes a career asset. Graduating with a curated, feedback-annotated portfolio is infinitely more valuable than a GPA when applying for creative roles. Our industry partnerships let students share their Folio profiles directly with employers who are tired of evaluating candidates through resumes alone.

name: Beacon
tagline: New career. No lottery ticket required.
description: Beacon runs intensive career transition bootcamps for mid-career professionals. Unlike traditional bootcamps aimed at recent grads, Beacon's programs are designed around the constraints of working adults — family obligations, existing skills to leverage, and the need for income continuity during the transition.
mission:
Career transitions are terrifying. You've spent ten years building expertise in one field, and now the market has shifted, your industry is shrinking, or you've simply realized you want something different. The options feel binary: quit your job and burn through savings in a bootcamp designed for 22-year-olds, or stay stuck and let resentment build.

Beacon was founded by three people who made mid-career transitions themselves — a former journalist turned product manager, an accountant turned data scientist, and a teacher turned software engineer. We know the specific fears: Will anyone hire a 35-year-old junior developer? Can I afford to take a pay cut? Will my existing experience count for anything? The answers are yes, you probably won't have to, and absolutely — but only if the transition is designed around your reality, not a college sophomore's.

Our bootcamps are structured for working professionals. Evening and weekend cohorts. Twelve to sixteen weeks. Curriculum that explicitly bridges from what you already know to what you need to learn. A marketing manager learning data analytics isn't starting from zero — they already understand business context, stakeholder communication, and strategic thinking. We build on those strengths instead of ignoring them.

Every Beacon graduate enters the job market with more than just new technical skills. Our career placement team works with each person to reframe their career narrative — not as someone starting over, but as someone bringing a unique combination of domain expertise and new capabilities that no 22-year-old bootcamp grad can match.

We measure success not by enrollment numbers but by placement rates and salary outcomes. If our graduates don't land roles they're excited about at compensation that respects their experience, we haven't done our job.
marketResearch:
The professional reskilling and career transition market is valued at $32 billion globally, driven by AI-induced displacement, industry consolidation, and increasing career mobility expectations among millennials and Gen X. The bootcamp segment specifically represents $5.8 billion, but the vast majority targets early-career learners. The mid-career transition niche — professionals with 8+ years of experience seeking to change fields — is severely underserved despite representing the fastest-growing segment of career changers. Our TAM is $5.8 billion in bootcamps, SAM of $2.1 billion targets career-change bootcamps for experienced professionals, and SOM of $180 million focuses on U.S. professionals transitioning into tech-adjacent roles.

General Assembly and Flatiron School dominate traditional bootcamps but design for early-career learners — their pace, pedagogy, and career support don't account for mid-career constraints. Springboard and Thinkful offer flexible online programs but lack the cohort intensity and career narrative work that career changers need. Corporate reskilling programs (Coursera for Business, Udacity Enterprise) serve employers, not individuals making voluntary transitions. Beacon differentiates through its exclusive focus on experienced professionals, part-time schedule design, and career narrative coaching.

Our target learner is 30-45, has 8-15 years of professional experience, household income of $70-120K, and is seeking to transition into product management, data analytics, UX design, or software engineering. They need flexibility (can't quit their day job), credibility (want employer recognition), and confidence (need to believe their experience is an asset). Average willingness to pay is $6,000-12,000 per program.

GTM strategy combines SEO content targeting career transition queries ("how to switch careers at 35"), LinkedIn thought leadership from our founders' personal transition stories, and alumni referrals. Corporate partnerships with companies laying off workers provide a talent pipeline with employer-sponsored tuition.

name: Syllabus
tagline: Curriculum design tools that respect teachers' time and expertise
description: Syllabus is a curriculum design platform for K-12 teachers that streamlines lesson planning, standards alignment, and resource organization. Built by former teachers who understand that planning shouldn't take longer than teaching.
mission:
Teaching is one of the most intellectually demanding jobs on earth, and curriculum design is the invisible engine that makes it work. Great teachers spend hours every week crafting lessons, finding resources, aligning to standards, differentiating for diverse learners, and adjusting plans based on what actually happened in class. Yet the tools they're given for this work are shocking — most teachers still plan in Word documents, Google Docs, or printed binder pages.

Syllabus was built by a team of former classroom teachers who spent as many evenings planning lessons as we did teaching them. We experienced firsthand the absurdity of aligning a lesson to seventeen different standards by hand, the frustration of losing a great activity because it was buried in last year's Google Drive, and the guilt of using someone else's worksheet because we simply ran out of time to create something better.

Our platform brings curriculum design into the modern era. Teachers build lesson plans with drag-and-drop components — warm-ups, direct instruction, activities, assessments — that automatically align to state and national standards. A built-in resource library lets teachers save, tag, and search everything they've ever created or collected. AI assists with the tedious parts — generating differentiated versions of activities, suggesting formative assessment questions, and identifying gaps in standards coverage across a unit.

Critically, we don't try to replace teacher judgment. Syllabus is a power tool for skilled professionals, not a lesson-plan generator for anyone with a pulse. Teachers remain the architects. We just give them better blueprints, sharper tools, and a workspace that doesn't make them want to scream.

Our north star is giving teachers back five hours a week — time that goes back to their families, their health, or the creative lesson design that drew them to teaching in the first place.
marketResearch:
The K-12 edtech market for teacher tools — including lesson planning, curriculum management, and instructional design — is valued at $4.6 billion, growing at 14% CAGR. Teachers in the U.S. spend an average of 7 hours per week on lesson planning and preparation, and 94% report spending personal funds on classroom resources. The market for purpose-built curriculum design tools is nascent, with most spending currently allocated to generic productivity tools or content marketplaces. Our TAM is $4.6 billion in K-12 teacher tools, SAM of $1.2 billion targets digital curriculum planning tools in English-speaking markets, and SOM of $85 million focuses on U.S. public school districts with 5,000+ students.

Current alternatives include Planbook (simple calendar-based planning, no AI or standards alignment), Teachers Pay Teachers (marketplace for resources, not a planning tool), and district-mandated curriculum platforms (rigid, top-down, despised by teachers). LMS platforms like Canvas and Schoology handle assignment distribution but not curriculum design. Syllabus differentiates by being the first platform that treats curriculum design as a professional practice — combining planning, standards alignment, resource management, and AI assistance in one workflow.

Our primary users are K-12 classroom teachers who take curriculum design seriously and are frustrated by inadequate tools. Early adopters are instructional coaches and curriculum coordinators who need to support teachers across a department or school. District-level buyers emerge when enough teachers within a district adopt Syllabus individually, creating bottom-up demand for institutional licenses.

GTM strategy follows a teacher-first viral model. Free individual accounts spread through teacher social media communities (Instagram teacher influencers, education Twitter, Facebook groups). School and district licenses are sold through instructional leadership — principals and curriculum directors who see teacher adoption data. Conference presence at ISTE, ASCD, and state-level education technology conferences builds credibility.

name: Cognia
tagline: Find what you don't know before the exam does
description: Cognia is an adaptive testing platform that identifies precise knowledge gaps in any subject area. Rather than scoring what you got right, Cognia maps what you don't know and generates a targeted study plan to fill those gaps before they cost you points.
mission:
Traditional tests are autopsy reports. They tell you what went wrong after the damage is done. You get a score, maybe see which questions you missed, and then you're on your own figuring out what to actually do about it. The problem isn't the test — it's the timing and the follow-through.

Cognia flips the model. Our adaptive assessments are designed not to grade you, but to diagnose you. Using item response theory and Bayesian knowledge modeling, each question is selected based on what will reveal the most about your understanding. A 20-minute Cognia assessment provides more diagnostic precision than a three-hour traditional exam because every question is chosen to maximize information about where your knowledge breaks down.

The output isn't a score. It's a knowledge map — a visual, topic-level breakdown showing exactly what you understand deeply, what you partially grasp, and what you've completely missed. Partial understanding is where Cognia shines. Most students don't have binary know-it-or-don't relationships with concepts. They understand the basics of photosynthesis but confuse the light and dark reactions. They can solve linear equations but fall apart with word problems. Cognia detects these nuances and builds study plans that target the specific sub-concepts where understanding breaks down.

We serve two audiences: students preparing for high-stakes exams who need to optimize limited study time, and instructors who want to understand where their class actually stands instead of waiting for the final exam to find out. For both, Cognia replaces guesswork with precision.

We believe assessment should be an act of care, not judgment. When it's done right, a test is a gift — it shows you exactly where to focus so you can grow as efficiently as possible.
marketResearch:
The assessment and testing market in education is valued at $18 billion, with formative and diagnostic assessment growing at 21% CAGR as educators shift from summative to learning-oriented testing. Adaptive testing specifically represents $2.8 billion, dominated by standardized test providers (ETS, College Board) and state assessment contractors. The niche of student-facing diagnostic assessment tools is smaller but growing rapidly at 35% CAGR. Our TAM is $2.8 billion in adaptive assessment, SAM of $900 million targets diagnostic assessment for college students and professional exam preppers, and SOM of $95 million focuses on U.S. students preparing for MCAT, LSAT, GRE, CPA, and similar high-stakes exams.

Competitors include UWorld (question banks with explanations but no adaptive diagnostics), Magoosh (test prep with basic analytics), and ALEKS (adaptive learning for math/chemistry, owned by McGraw-Hill). Standardized testing companies offer practice tests but not diagnostic assessments designed to reveal specific knowledge gaps. Cognia differentiates through its diagnostic-first approach — the purpose isn't to simulate the test but to surgically identify gaps — and its Bayesian modeling that provides confidence intervals on each topic's mastery level.

Our primary users are students preparing for graduate admissions exams (MCAT, LSAT, GRE), professional certifications (CPA, CFA, bar exam), and challenging undergraduate courses. These students face enormous content volumes and limited time — they need to know exactly where to focus. Secondary users are university instructors who want mid-semester diagnostic data on their class.

GTM strategy targets high-stakes exam prep communities through content marketing (study strategy blogs), Reddit and Discord community engagement, and partnerships with tutoring companies that use Cognia diagnostics to guide their sessions. Student referrals drive organic growth — when a study group discovers Cognia, the entire group adopts it.

name: Atelier
description: Atelier is a platform for live, cohort-based courses taught by working creative professionals. Unlike pre-recorded content, Atelier courses are taught in real-time with small groups, peer feedback, and direct access to instructors who are actively practicing their craft.
mission:
The internet promised to democratize education, and in some ways it delivered. You can learn almost anything from YouTube and online courses. But the dirty secret of self-paced online learning is that almost nobody finishes. Completion rates for MOOCs hover around 5%. The content is there. The motivation isn't. And for creative skills — writing, design, illustration, photography, filmmaking — the feedback loop that self-paced learning can't provide is often more important than the content itself.

Atelier exists because creative learning is inherently social. The workshop model — small groups, live instruction, peer critique, iterative projects — has produced great artists, designers, and writers for centuries. We're bringing that model online with the production quality and accessibility that the internet makes possible.

Every Atelier course is taught live by a working professional, not a career educator. Our instructors are practicing designers at studios, published authors, exhibited photographers, and working filmmakers. They teach from current experience, share real client work as case studies, and provide the kind of candid industry feedback that no pre-recorded course can offer. Classes are capped at 20 students to ensure everyone participates, gets feedback, and builds genuine connections with their cohort.

The cohort model solves the completion problem. When you're learning alongside 19 peers who see your work, give you feedback, and expect you to show up, the social accountability transforms outcomes. Our completion rate is 87% — not because we've gamified engagement, but because humans are wired to show up for other humans.

We started with creative disciplines because the feedback loop is most critical there, but the cohort-based live learning model applies to any skill where practice and critique matter more than information transfer. We're building the future of professional education — and it looks a lot like the past, reimagined for the internet.
marketResearch:
The online professional education market is valued at $46 billion, but cohort-based course platforms (CBCs) represent a rapidly growing segment estimated at $1.2 billion, growing at 40%+ CAGR. The shift from self-paced to live learning is driven by employer demand for practical skills and learner demand for accountability and community. Our TAM encompasses the $1.2 billion CBC market, SAM of $480 million targets creative and professional skills courses for English-speaking adults, and SOM of $65 million focuses on design, writing, photography, and illustration courses for working professionals in North America and Europe.

Maven (founded by Gagan Biyani and Wes Kao) pioneered the cohort-based platform model but focuses broadly across business, tech, and creative skills. Skillshare offers creative courses but in a pre-recorded, self-paced format with low completion rates. MasterClass provides celebrity-taught content with no interactivity. Domestika offers high-quality creative courses but without live components. Atelier differentiates through its exclusive focus on creative professionals, strict 20-person cohort caps, and instructor-as-practitioner model that ensures teaching stays grounded in current industry practice.

Our primary students are creative professionals with 2-8 years of experience who want to level up specific skills — a graphic designer learning motion design, a writer exploring screenwriting, or a photographer transitioning to directing. These professionals earn $50-120K and are willing to invest $300-800 per course for high-quality live instruction. Secondary students include career changers entering creative fields and hobbyists seeking structured community.

GTM strategy leverages instructor audiences. Each Atelier instructor brings their existing social following (typically 10K-500K across Instagram, YouTube, and newsletters). We provide production support, curriculum design assistance, and a platform — they bring students and credibility. This instructor-led distribution keeps customer acquisition costs low while building a content moat that's impossible to replicate with pre-recorded courses.
